Analytic Cauchy data on small polydiscs

Original exposition and proofs: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. CC0.

A differential equation can lose derivatives at each successive substitution. For analytic functions, the distance to the complex boundary measures this loss. Integration with zero initial data supplies an opposing gain. Keeping both estimates at the same boundary weight gives a convergent construction with an explicit domain and error bound.

We first solve a mixed derivative problem with data on several coordinate faces. A thin rescaling then gives the local analytic Cauchy theorem on a noncharacteristic coordinate hyperplane. The coefficients may be complex and need not have real characteristic roots.

Throughout this lesson means the ordinary complex derivative, without a factor of . Put Here , and a multiindex has nonnegative integer entries. Norms are suprema over the indicated open domains and are used only when finite.

The supplied complex contour proofs, Sections 16.1–16.3, prove the circle formula, every Cauchy derivative estimate, joint power series on products of disks, parameter integration and convergence of all derivatives under locally uniform holomorphic convergence. Their scalar calculus and integration foundations provide the real integrals and uniform convergence used below.

Proof. In one coordinate let . On each compact subpolydisc, the integral and all differentiated integrands are bounded. The contour prerequisite therefore proves holomorphy. The one-variable primitive formula gives , and at .

Repeated integration in that coordinate gives To check the factor, write the repeated integrals as integrals over , integrate the outer variables for fixed , and use their simplex volume . That volume follows by induction from integrating . Compact absolute bounds justify every interchange. Primitives in different coordinates commute by the same finite Fubini argument. Thus , which proves (A3), its equation and all face conditions. Integrating each weight gives , proving (A4).

For uniqueness, expand a homogeneous solution as its joint Taylor series at the origin. Condition (A2) makes the coefficient of zero whenever some : choose in that face condition and compare the remaining Taylor coefficients. For , the coefficient in is , so it too vanishes. The function vanishes near zero and hence throughout the polydisc. The joint identity principle used here follows directly from the joint Taylor expansion: the set of points with a zero neighborhood is open; at a limit point, continuity of every derivative makes all Taylor coefficients zero, so it is relatively closed. Connectedness finishes the argument. This also proves uniqueness for germs.

Corollary 6 (local analytic Cauchy existence). Let a scalar differential operator of total order have analytic coefficients near zero in . Suppose the coefficient of is nonzero at zero. For analytic and analytic data near zero, there is a unique analytic solution germ with The statement also holds directly for holomorphic germs.

Proof. A convergent real power series has a holomorphic extension to a sufficiently small complex polydisc: absolute convergence on a smaller polydisc follows from its convergence radius, and termwise differentiation follows on still smaller polydiscs by the same geometric bounds as the contour prerequisite. Use these extensions for all the finitely many coefficients and data. The leading coefficient remains nonzero after shrinking, by continuity; its reciprocal is holomorphic by the quotient differentiation rule. Divide the equation by it, giving (A21) with a correspondingly divided forcing.

Choose so that the closed polydisc lies in the common holomorphic neighborhood. All its coefficients are then bounded there. For with , necessarily . Every exponent of in (A22) is therefore positive. With fixed, the finite weighted coefficient sum tends to zero uniformly as , using the bounds on . Thus some satisfies (A22).

To impose the data, put The polynomial in has exactly the prescribed normal jets. On the chosen closed polydisc, after a further initial shrink if needed, every tangential derivative of the data appearing in is bounded. Hence the residual forcing is bounded on the input polydisc; Theorem 5 supplies with zero normal jets. The same theorem and Theorem 4 give uniqueness of germs. Restriction to real variables gives the real analytic assertion; for real coefficients and real data, conjugating the holomorphic extension and its variables gives another solution with the same jets, so uniqueness makes the restriction real.

If the normalized coefficients already satisfy (A22), the nonzero-data estimate is obtained by replacing in (A23) with and bounding by on the output domain. Bounded values of on an open disk alone do not bound every derivative on that entire disk; choosing a smaller closed input polydisc in the proof is essential.

Exercise 4 (intermediate) — a sufficient bound need not be necessary. Solve with , for any complex , and determine its domain of holomorphy.

Solution. The series converges uniformly on every compact subset of : the absolute term ratio is at most , which tends uniformly to zero on such a compact set. It is entire, and all derivatives may be taken termwise on compact subsets. The differentiated term is , and reindexing the remaining differentiated terms gives . Both face values vanish. Its Taylor coefficients are forced recursively by the equation and face data, proving uniqueness of an analytic germ and hence of any entire solution with these data. Theorem 4 only gives a sufficient smallness condition; failure of that condition is not a nonexistence conclusion.
